frus-1861-d9:
A dispatch from Joseph Wright reached Secretary of State William H. Seward under the date 8 June 1861. It is document 9 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June found the Union raising armies and the Confederacy seeking friends abroad. Reports like Wright's helped Washington gauge which governments might aid the South. Alone, one letter says little, but the run of them formed the picture on which Seward acted. The run of Wright letters ends in June, which gives his file a neat, brief shape. His file is brief, yet its dates span the whole first act of the war abroad.
frus-1862-d9:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Charles Francis Adams, dated 24 January 1862. Congress received it as Document 9 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d9:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 9 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

December found London full of war talk. France had floated the idea that the great powers step in to stop the fight, and Britain's choice on that plan mattered greatly to Washington. Adams's letters tracked each turn of that talk. This dispatch is part of the watch, written by the man whose calm hand in London did the Union much good.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d9: President Roosevelt sent word to Marshal Stalin on June 18, 1943, the same day he also wrote to Churchill. The Stalin letter is Document 9 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Mid-June found the president balancing both allies at once as plans for the year took shape. No subject is stated in the record, so the letter must speak for itself in the printed text of the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d9:
Prime Minister Churchill sent this message to President Roosevelt on June 1, 1944, five days before the Normandy landings. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume's correspondence leading to the September conference.

A Churchill letter dated June 1 sits in history's anteroom: everything in the Western war was about to be tested. The Prime Minister, who had championed and feared the invasion by turns, kept writing to Washington as the fleet assembled. For readers, the message gains its force from its date alone, a leader's words written on the edge of the decisive operation of the war in Europe.
frus-1945-50-intel-d9:
Donovan wrote to President Truman again on 13 September 1945, pressing his case for a central intelligence service. He had one week left as head of the OSS, though the end had not yet been announced. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A second direct appeal in three weeks shows Donovan knew his cause was slipping. Truman favored a smaller, cheaper setup and distrusted a peacetime spy agency on the wartime scale. This memorandum is thus a document of a losing campaign, written by a man who had built much and was about to watch it dissolved. Readers can measure, in the volume's next papers, exactly how far the president's choice fell short of what Donovan asked.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d9: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on 8 October 1944, answering within days during a busy month of summit preparation. His message is document 9 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. The fall exchanges among the three leaders set the stage for the decisions they would face together in the Crimea the following February.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d9:
Truman thanked Churchill for his estimate of Europe's future in this telegram of May 14, 1945. From the present point of view, he wrote, no conjecture was possible about what the Soviets might do. Germany would soon sit under small occupation forces, while the great part of Western armies fought Japan in the Orient.

He agreed fully that an early tripartite meeting was necessary to reach an understanding with Russia. But a report from the embassies in Moscow seemed necessary first, before deciding time or place. He had talked with Eden that day. He would make every practicable effort to arrange his affairs for an early meeting somewhere.
tob-0039-d9:
Roll 10 of the Doctors' Trial microfilm holds a further section of the verbatim transcript from Nuremberg, 1946 to 1947. The defendants, physicians and administrators of Nazi Germany, faced charges built on camp experiments. The record runs to thousands of pages across the full set.

Here the proceedings continue in their working order: witnesses called, documents marked, counsel heard, the bench ruling as disputes arise. No editor smooths the story, which is why historians trust the transcript. The case it records ended in convictions and in a new code for medical research. This roll forms one link in the chain of that record, preserved entire for study.
